birthplace: 118 Duke Street, Liverpool, in a family of Welsh descent; raised from about the age of seven at Gwrych near Abergele in Denbighshire
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English by birth and Welsh by upbringing and self-identification; the popular lyric, metrical romance and devotional verse of the later Romantic period, and the literary annual and gift-book public that made it
literary_identity: The most extensively read and reprinted woman poet of the nineteenth century in Britain and America, and the first to build a complete professional authorship on the lyric of domestic affection; a contributor of verse and prose to every leading magazine and annual of her day, and the settled authority for a whole repertoire of women's feeling.
biography: Hemans was born at Liverpool on 25 September 1793, the daughter of George Browne, a merchant whose affairs failed at the turn of the century, and of a mother whose father had held a foreign consular appointment in the same city; when the girl was about seven the family removed to Gwrych, near Abergele in the Welsh north, and the scenery and the Welsh claims of her childhood stay visible throughout her work and in her own account of herself. She was educated largely at home, an avid and early reader with an unusual memory for verse, and by about 1808 she was contributing poems to a popular monthly magazine; her first collected volume, declaring domestic affection as the durable ground of happiness, appeared in 1812. In that year she married an army officer of Welsh birth, Captain Hemans, a Peninsular-war survivor several years her senior, and within the next few years she bore him a family of sons; about 1818 her husband quitted England for the continent and did not return, and from her twenties until her death she maintained herself and her children wholly by her pen. The following decades made her the leading female poet of the day: volumes of lyric and occasional verse, translations and imitations from the Romance languages, metrical tales, and in 1825 the ambitious Spenserian romance of a child preserved within a monastic retreat. Records of Woman of 1828, whose title names a design rather than a poem, consolidated her authority over the history of women's feeling and drew a substantial notice in the Edinburgh review; Songs of the Affections followed in 1830, gathering the shorter manner of her last decade. Her homes moved from Wales to the neighbourhood of Liverpool, where she rented in the later years, and finally to Dublin, in which city she had lived at an earlier period of her married life; her income came from the annuals and the magazines, and from an American market which reprinted her faster than any copyright could follow. Her health, never robust, gave way under overwork, anxiety about her sons and private grief, and she died at her lodging in Dublin on 16 May 1835, in her forty-second year, and was buried in the vault of the Dublin church near her house. The collected editions, one of them with a memoir prepared by a member of her family, and the interminable reprints in gift-books, schoolbooks, hymnals and recitation collections, kept her lines before the English-speaking world for the rest of the century; her dismissal by high modernist taste as merely sentimental, and her recovery by later scholarship on women's writing, are both part of her recorded history.
literary_profile: Her canon runs to many separate volumes and includes the lyric meditation and song, the short dramatic address in a historical or imaginary woman's voice, the metrical tale and romance, the devotional hymn and sacred poem, the topographical and national piece, and translations or imitations from Spanish and Italian sources; her prose is slight beside her verse, and a great deal of that verse was made to order for the annuals, often written to accompany a specified engraving. Her characteristic single poem builds upon one emblem, one farewell or one grave, and develops it as a meditation; the longer narrative poems of the middle years, of which The Forest Sanctuary is the example, are her attempt to be read as a moral poet of sustained design. Posthumous collections gathered what the market had demanded, and the arrangement of her volumes by length and tone rather than by plan is itself evidence of her relation to her publishers.
stylistic_characteristics: A deliberately vocal and singable smoothness, in common and short iambic measure with marked refrains, adapted to recitation and to musical setting; the closed heroic couplet used where feeling is to settle into maxim; personification, apostrophe and the address to an absent or dead beloved; an emblematic method in which a token, a lamp, a bracelet or a bird carries the whole argument; historical and Romance colouring softened to a domestic and moral use; and a pathos concentrated on a single situation, which contemporaries found overpowering and later critics found repetitive.
intellectual_concerns: Affection tried by separation, bereavement and time, and its survival as the ground of identity; the destinies, claims and education of women, and the mind set against the lot allowed it; constancy, forbearance and jealousy recorded as history; Providence, gratitude and vocation in the poem of preservation; consolation and the hope of reunion after death; exile and homelessness; Catholic and legendary Romance matter subdued to a plainly Protestant devotional temper; national memory, Wales and the scenery of childhood.
historical_significance: She made the woman poet a mass-market professional figure, and the idiom of her affectionate and mourning lyric became the ordinary language of Victorian domestic and devotional culture, quoted, paraphrased and set to music without attribution for generations. Her career is the clearest record of the economics of the literary annual before it reached its full height, and of the transatlantic circulation that could support a British writer's income. The design of Records of Woman gave the century a durable subject and a set of transferable female personae, and the sequence of her reputation - enormous fame, modernist dismissal, and recovery by feminist scholarship from the late twentieth century - is now a standard case in the history of canon formation and of the gendering of literary value.
major_influences: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
biographical_uncertainty: Her birthplace and her national identity are given variously in the authorities: the register evidence places her birth in Duke Street, Liverpool, in September 1793, while a strong Welsh tradition, resting on her upbringing and on her own identification, has claimed her as Welsh, and older handbook accounts sometimes misdate the month of her birth. The christian name of the officer she married is given by most modern sources as Alfred, though some catalogue traditions style her by the other name; the date and terms of the separation, and the number and survival of her sons, rest largely on family and later testimony; the nature of the illness that killed her is variously described; and how much editorial control she exercised over the posthumous collections, and what share her family's memoir has in shaping the record of her life, cannot be determined.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the metropolitan periodical and literary-annual public of the later Romantic period, and the verse romance and short lyric of the 1820s and 1830s
literary_identity: Poet, critic and novelist: the first English woman of letters to make a complete living by periodical verse and review, the controlling presence in the poetical pages of a leading weekly paper for well over a decade, and the creator of the persona of the gifted, wounded and professional woman poet that the annuals made canonical.
biography: Landon was born at Hans Place in Chelsea on 14 August 1802, the daughter of John Landon, at that time a partner in an army agency house and a traveller in his youth to Africa and the West Indies, and of Catherine Jane Bishop; a precocious child, she was educated at home and by her own reading rather than by any regular schooling, and began to publish verse in the magazines about 1820. Her contributions to a widely circulated weekly literary paper, and above all the poetical notices and reviews which she wrote over her initials, gave her at once a name and a critical power unusual for a woman of her years; the first volume, issued in 1821 under her own name rather than over initials, announced the situations of her whole career, and the volume of 1824, named for its long poem on the Italian singer-poetess, made her famous. Her father's death in 1824 left the family relatively poor and she became its support, a responsibility she carried for the rest of her life; about the end of the decade losses sustained by the household through the impositions of an unscrupulous man, and the public trial that followed, exposed her to a gossip about her judgement and her conduct that never entirely subsided. Through the later 1820s and the 1830s she remained the annuals' most constant and most imitated poet, publishing a series of verse romances of which The Golden Violet and The Venetian Bracelet are examples, and turning increasingly to prose fiction, with three novels of romance and historical matter appearing between the early and the late 1830s, alongside a large quantity of magazine verse and review. Her position as a woman who judged other people's poetry, and who was paid for it, made her a target of personal attack in the periodical press of the 1830s, and soon after the volume of 1829 the house that had published her earlier romances closed its engagement with her; the reading of her verse as confession, which her market encouraged, turned her private affiliations and her broken engagements into public knowledge. In 1837, in her thirty-fifth year, she married George Maclean, a Scotsman in the service of the British settlement on the Gold Coast of West Africa, and she quitted England for that station in the summer of 1838. She died at Cape Coast Castle on 15 October 1838, aged thirty-six, having been in Africa only a few months, and was buried at the castle; an empty phial of prussic acid was found with her, and the verdict of the inquest, which took note of the medicine she had been taking, returned accidental self-poisoning, while report has never stopped arguing the case. Her collected verse appeared after her death with a memoir of her life, and her name stayed before readers through the middle decades of the century before a long eclipse from which modern scholarship and modern editions have brought her back.
literary_profile: Her work divides between the long verse romance in stanzas, drawing on chivalric, Italian and legendary matter and interrupted by personal comment; the short lyric and sonnet-like piece written for the annual and often in company with an engraving; the critical and descriptive prose on poetry and on the literature of the day; and the three novels of romance and historical fiction of the later years. She left also a large body of magazine verse, much of it first printed over her initials and gathered afterwards into volumes, and a correspondence which is a record of the professional writer's life. The characteristic structure is a situation of pledged and misread feeling worked out in a token or an emblem, and the characteristic persona is the woman of genius whose gift is at once her fame and her exposure.
stylistic_characteristics: A stanzic iambic measure of rapid declamatory movement, much given to triple time, refrained closings and an enjambed talky ease, plainly tuned for recitation; compressed direct address and apostrophe in the shorter lyrics; an emblematic method in which a bracelet, a veil, a flower or a picture carries the argument and turns against the person who wears it; historical and local colour used as the scenery of feeling rather than as antiquarian display; and a sustained irony, usually unintended by its first readers, between the confessional voice and the commercial occasion that required it.
intellectual_concerns: The woman artist's vocation and its price; fame purchased by self-exposure; constancy, desertion and jealousy as social rather than private facts; the symbol that pledges love and then accuses; the inheritance of romance and chivalry converted into a grammar of feminine feeling; poverty, dependence and the economics of professional authorship for a woman with a family to maintain; exile, travel and the European south; early death and the mourning of poets.
historical_significance: She defined the possibility of a full-time women's literary career in the periodical market, at once the annuals' typical contributor and their most powerful editor of taste, and she supplied the nineteenth century with its most influential image of the woman poet as popular artist and victim, a figure reworked by later novelists and poets. Her practice fixed the short lyric of the keepsake as a serious form and made the emblematic token a lasting device of gift-book writing. Her death became at once a scandal and a literary event, and the recovery of her work by modern scholarship has made her central to the history of Romantic authorship, of women's professional writing and of the transatlantic book trade.
major_influences: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
biographical_uncertainty: The circumstances of her death remain genuinely disputed: the phial of prussic acid, the medicine she had been prescribed for illness, the verdict of accidental self-poisoning, the rumours of deliberate suicide and of despair over her marriage, and the possible share of other parties cannot be resolved on the surviving evidence, and the account given by her husband and by her friends is necessarily interested. Her childhood residences and the extent of her formal education are imperfectly recorded; the details of the family's financial losses in the later 1820s and of the trial that followed are reported with large inconsistencies; the story of her broken engagements rests on letters and on later memoir; and the division between her public persona and her private feelings, which her contemporaries read as one text, is the permanent difficulty of her biography.

birthplace: Newington Green, Middlesex, on the northern edge of London (some authorities say the adjacent Stoke Newington), in a prosperous Unitarian family
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the eighteenth-century didactic and topographical tradition carried on within the Romantic period, and the polite London letters of the Regency and post-Regency decades
literary_identity: Banker by profession and poet by vocation: the most honoured of those Romantic-era verse-writers who stood outside the Lake and Byronic schools, the last great practitioner of the reflective heroic couplet, and the host of the most celebrated breakfast table in the literary history of London.
biography: Rogers was born at Newington Green on 30 July 1763, the third son of a Unitarian family of large means, and was educated at dissenting schools in the neighbourhood of London rather than at a university. He was put early into business and became a partner in a London house, and on his father's death he inherited enough to withdraw from active trade and to live in London as a man of letters, a collector and a patron. His first considerable poem, an essay on the pleasures of recollection, appeared in 1792 and went through many editions, while the verse of his student years was quietly suppressed. For decades he was the centre of a famous weekly breakfast table at his house in St James's Place, where statesmen, actors, painters, publishers and poets of every party sat together, and where the conversation which was reported after his death as his Table Talk took shape. He twice travelled in Italy after the Napoleonic wars reopened the continent to English visitors, and those journeys supplied the matter of the topographical poem published anonymously in part in 1822 and completed under his own name in the later 1820s; an early disappointed attachment and the deaths of friends return through it as the loss which reflective verse attempts to console. He lived unmarried, on terms of closeness with his sister and with a small circle of friends, and passed his last years between London and the continent, taking a formal part in the affairs of the national collection of painting, of which he was a trustee from 1834 until his death. When the laureateship fell at the death of the elder poet of the Lakes in 1850 he was approached, refused the honour on the ground of his years, and named a younger successor who accepted it. His collected Poems of 1827, revised and re-set from the separate issues of 1792, 1819 and 1822, gave him at last the single authoritative form in which he was read for the rest of the century; he died in London on 18 December 1855, aged ninety-two, and the record of his talk and of his generosity to poorer writers and to imprisoned Italian liberals was published by his friends in the years immediately following.
literary_profile: His printed work is deliberately small and elaborately made: two long reflective poems on common life and on Italy, a shorter earlier poem on memory, and a company of lyrics, ballads, hymn-like pieces, romances and translations, many of them intercalated into the longer structures or first sold to the keepsake and magazine market. He wrote no prose book of his own; his prose remains is the reported table-talk and the letters, and his serious editorship was exercised on his own texts, of which he left several substantially different states. The characteristic poem is a meditative progress in couplets, interrupted by a song, in which an observed scene or a remembered person is raised to a general reflection on ordinary experience.
stylistic_characteristics: Closed and heavily pointed heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, descended from the eighteenth-century schools rather than from the blank verse of his contemporaries; a diction of polish, reticence and understatement, avoiding archaism, technical vocabulary and experiment; epigrammatic and sententious closure, balanced antithesis, and a strong sense of the audible line for recitation; contrasted with these, in the intercalated songs and ballads, a light and genuinely tuneful lyrical measure which was widely set and widely imitated. Revision is the visible method: the printed text is the residue of many cancelled draft states, and the reticence of the surface is the product of labour rather than of ease.
intellectual_concerns: The dignity of ordinary and domestic life as a subject for serious verse; memory, attachment and the consolation of the bereaved; taste, decorum and the rules of an inherited metre; religion of a liberal and anti-sectarian kind, with a sympathetic but unconverted interest in Catholic ceremony; exile, political imprisonment and the claims of liberty on the poet's purse; the moral uses of painting and of the Italian landscape; the poet's duty to a reading public that buys the annual rather than the subscription volume.
historical_significance: For half a century he was the standard instance of a poet who could be ranked with the first generation of the Romantic school without belonging to it, and his refusal of the exotic and the heroic was a live alternative to Wordsworthian simplicity and to Byronic rhetoric. His Italy was for much of the nineteenth century the usual English poem about Italy, and the illustrated editions that paired it with engraved landscape vignettes made it a defining object of the gift-book market. His breakfast table and the Table Talk reported from it are a primary record of the social life of Romantic letters and an indispensable source of anecdote about the greater poets of the age; and the rise and disappearance of his reputation is a standing case study in Victorian and modern canon formation.
biographical_uncertainty: His birthplace is reported variously as Newington Green and as Stoke Newington, and the boundary between the two makes the difference one of naming rather than of fact; the details of his schooling and of his years in the banking house are thinly documented; and the identity and chronology of the early attachment that lies behind the mournful passages of his Italian poem rest largely on the recollection of friends.

birthplace: Glasgow, in the house in the High Street of a merchant family which claimed Argyllshire descent
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish, working within a British public; popular narrative and lyric verse of the war decades and of the Regency, and the Edinburgh-and-London publishing world that connected them
literary_identity: Poet, anthologist and literary manager: the Scottish contributor to the popular Romantic bestseller list, a maker of nationally remembered lyrics and metrical romances, the editor whose selections taught a century its own poetic history, and one of the promoters of the metropolitan university founded in the 1820s.
biography: Campbell was born in Glasgow on 27 July 1777, the youngest of the eleven children of Alexander Campbell, a merchant whose fortunes were destroyed by the losses of the American war, and his childhood was shaped by a ruined family's shift to modest dependence in the west of Scotland. He was educated at school in Glasgow and for a time at the university there, was placed young in a counting house, and then earned his living as a private tutor, with a period of service in the Highlands, before he gave himself wholly to letters; a few schoolboy verses were printed before he was twenty. The Pleasures of Hope appeared in 1799, when its author was twenty-two, and made his reputation at once and at large; enlarged editions, with the shorter poems that were soon recited everywhere, followed through the next two decades. He removed to London in 1801, endured several years of pressing poverty, and then established himself as a professed man of letters by his pen, by his friendships with the leading writers of the day and by his management of his own publishing interests. Gertrude of Wyoming in 1809 made him the most widely read narrator of romantic verse before the vogue of the metrical tales of his senior friends, and his lyrics of the war years passed into ordinary recitation and into schoolbooks. His Specimens of the British Poets of 1819, a work of selection rather than of scholarship, gave him a second career as the period's popular historian of English verse, and he was at once a proprietor and conductor of one of the leading monthlies and the busiest of the poets in the London book trade. Later recognition came from several directions: government acknowledgement of his standing, wide subscription support for his collected verse, and a share, vigorously promoted in print and at public meetings, in the foundation of the metropolitan university. He was a friend and correspondent of the leading Scottish and English writers of his generation, a habitual visitor to the continent, and an unremitting worker for funds for distressed authors and their families; he died away from home, at Boulogne, on 15 June 1844, and was buried in Westminster Abbey among the poets, his funeral attended by friends and by foreign admirers of his poems of national liberty.
literary_profile: His work falls into four recognisable groups: the didactic and reflective poem in couplets, of which The Pleasures of Hope is the example; the metrical romance or tale, of which Gertrude of Wyoming is the most successful; the short patriotic, maritime and elegiac lyric intended for recitation and for the singing clubs; and the editorial and critical prose of the Specimens and its separately circulated biographical notices. He wrote steadily for magazines and annuals, conducted correspondence on literary business on a large scale, and left a considerable body of letters. Sustained ambition to a larger epic design was a permanent and unfulfilled part of his career, and his later volumes repeat and vary the situations of the earlier ones.
stylistic_characteristics: An instinct for the line that can be heard, quoted and sung, worked out in common and short measure stanzas with marked refrains and an easy command of ballad movement; the inherited heroic couplet of the eighteenth-century didactic poem used with spirit in the longer argumentative work; Spenserian stanzas for romance, with an archaising dignity that reviewers debated; a plain, earnest and frequently rhetorical diction, relying on a single strong situation of pathos rather than on subtlety of thought, and much given to the sententious closing line that passes into proverb.
intellectual_concerns: Hope, moral progress and the education of the species; national liberty and the fate of small and injured peoples, Poland and Ireland among them; the claims of Scotland and its scenery within a British literature; domestic affection tested by violence and death; the transatlantic frontier and the fate of its first inhabitants thought in the sentimental vocabulary of the age; the formation of a national poetic canon and the material condition of the writer who lives by it.
historical_significance: He showed that the couplet didactic poem of the previous century could still be an immediate bestseller in the 1790s, and that a Scottish poet of the Romantic generation could reach the widest popular audience of all by combining revolutionary hope with domestic romance. Gertrude of Wyoming carried popular verse from border matter to American colonial subject and was reprinted across the United States, and his lyrics and songs long held a place in recitation, in the schoolbook and in the national memory of the war years. As editor of the Specimens he was for two generations the ordinary introduction to the earlier English and Scottish poets, and as a public worker he helped to make the writer's trade respectable and institutional. The subsequent eclipse of his reputation is itself a much-cited instance of Romantic canon formation and its later revisions.
biographical_uncertainty: The family's claimed Argyllshire descent rests largely on the poet's own account and on the memoir made after his death; the dates of his university attendance and of his employment as clerk and as tutor are unevenly recorded; the year of his final settlement in London is variously given as 1800 or 1801; and the sums and dates of the subscription income and of official financial recognition differ between the biographies.

birthplace: 12 Aungier Street, Dublin, only son of a grocer and wine merchant of the city who later held office as a magistrate there
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish, working for a metropolitan British public; the Irish national lyric and song tradition, the Whig-liberal and emancipation cause, and the fashionable Oriental and satirical verse of the Regency
literary_identity: Poet, lyricist, satirist, editor and biographer: in his own lifetime the most widely known and most lucratively published of the Romantic poets, the maker of the national air set to modern words, and the assumed national bard of Ireland who ended his life in an English country cottage.
biography: Moore was born in Dublin on 28 May 1779, the only son of a grocer and wine merchant who rose to municipal office in the city, and he showed such early facility in verse that his college years at Trinity, to which he entered in 1794, were remembered for his printed attempts rather than for his reading. He quitted Ireland for London about the turn of the century, established himself by his pen, and published in those first years translations of the Anacreontic poems and a small collection put out under the name of a fictitious deceased author. He was received in society and in the drawing rooms, moved in the theatre and publishing world, and became the most sought-after lyric writer of the Regency, supplying words to recovered Irish airs in a serial publication that grew through more than two decades into a national monument in song; his satires on the London society he lived in, a sequence of intercepted verse epistles of 1813 and the comic tourist letters of 1818, were issued under the name of a young Irish correspondent, a disguise that answered the risk of libel and sharpened the outsider's eye on English vanity. Lalla Rookh of 1817, with its framed Oriental romances, brought him a publisher's fee of three thousand guineas and a European fame that no poem of his second decade exceeded, and the religious narrative of the angel lovers which followed in 1822 drew upon him the loudest borrowing controversy of his career. His friendship with the greater poet of the generation, begun in London, cooled and revived, was renewed in Italy, where Moore visited him in the last years at Venice and at the towns of the Adriatic and the Ligurian coast, and it ended in the office of literary executor which he accepted and in the suppression and burning of the dead man's memoirs in the publisher's rooms in May 1824, a transaction in which the sums exchanged and the shares of the parties were reported differently by each of them. He printed a defence of Byron's poetry against clerical attack and, after long delay, the Letters and Journals with Notices of his Life in 1830, the book on which the century's knowledge of its subject chiefly rested. He had married in 1811 a woman whose family connections gave him entry to the professional gentry, and from 1818 his home was Sloperton Cottage near Bromham in Wiltshire, where he lived, honoured at home and abroad but reproached by a younger school of Irish writers for the moderation of his lyrics, until his death; his later labour was largely prose, a life of the Irish dramatist of the previous generation, a history of Ireland carried through several volumes, and a vast correspondence, and his own papers were edited and published after his death by the statesman who had been his friend. He outlived the children of his marriage, several of whom died in youth, and that grief darkens the record of his last years; he died at Sloperton on 25 February 1852 and was buried in the churchyard of the next village, a long way from Dublin.
literary_profile: His work has five distinct departments: the serial national lyrics and songs written to airs; the Oriental and romantic narrative in verse, of which Lalla Rookh is the centre; the light satirical verse epistle and comic poem; the devotional and religious narrative and hymn; and the editorial, biographical and historical prose, including the Byron correspondence and memoirs, the life of the dramatist, the history of his country and his own posthumous autobiography. He was also a performing musician who sang and accompanied his own songs, and much of his verse was made for the voice rather than for the page. The habitual form is the short dramatic lyric or the ornamental narrative divided into easily detached pieces, and his prose is the same gift of easy narration carried into biography.
stylistic_characteristics: Lyric measures of exceptional fluency, often in triple time and built on refrains and on the requirements of a pre-existing air, with a vocabulary of tenderness and national regret; in the romances a richly coloured and sensuous descriptive style, anapestic and musical, depending on scenery and on effect rather than on analysis; in the satire an easy decasyllabic and octosyllabic couplet of the Augustan familiar school, carried by gossip, insinuation and feigned simplicity; in the religious poem an unction of address and apostrophe which contemporary critics found either affecting or mercenary. Facility, finish and a constant attention to the ear are his permanent characteristics, and the same qualities, to later judges, are his limitation.
intellectual_concerns: The survival of a conquered nation in its music, its memory and its lost causes; religious zeal, imposture and fanaticism as the motives of history, and the possibility of a holiness preserved through temptation; emancipation, toleration and the civic claims of Irish Catholics; the ethics of editorial discretion, friendship and the keeping of dead men's secrets; exile, travel and the southern sojourn; the commerce between cultural nationalism and the metropolitan market that pays for it; the relations of words to music, and of song to poetry.
historical_significance: He made the recovered national air a European form and gave Ireland the song repertory by which the nineteenth century imagined it, at the cost of a lasting argument about compromise and authenticity. As the best-paid and most translated poet of his generation he demonstrates the commercial possibilities open to Romantic verse before the annuals reached their height, and his Fudge Family letters long remained the template of tourists' satire. His edition and memoir of the greater poet of the generation founded the serious editing of literary correspondence and, in the suppression of the memoirs, supplied the canonical case in the history of editorial ethics and of literary reputation. His late eclipse, while a dozen of his lyrics stayed in the recital and schoolbook repertory, is a standard illustration of the severance between popular Romantic fame and modern canon.
major_influences: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
biographical_uncertainty: The family's religious history and Moore's own communion are variously represented in the biographies, which reflect his Catholic Irish origins and his Anglican connections; the exact sums paid and received over the suppression of the memoirs, and how much of that manuscript he had seen, copied or destroyed, are still argued from party statements; the chronology of his Italian journeys of the later 1810s and early 1820s is given differently in the standard accounts; and the authenticity of several airs and of his own share in their arrangements remains a matter of musicological dispute.
